questions.prompt: In infrastructure as code, what does it mean for a tool to be declarative rather than imperative?
options: It describes the desired end state, and the tool figures out what needs to change to reach it
It lists an ordered sequence of steps to execute exactly once
It requires manually clicking through a console in a specific order
It only works with cloud providers whose APIs are idempotent
It means the configuration file must be written in JSON rather than a custom language
It means every resource must be destroyed and recreated from scratch on every run
questions.explain: A declarative tool like Terraform or Bicep describes the end state you want — a storage account named X, in region Y, with these settings — and the tool itself computes what needs to be created, changed, or left alone to reach that state. Run it again unchanged, and nothing happens.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an imperative script, like an Azure CLI script running `az storage account create`, which is the exact opposite of declarative — it's an ordered list of steps to run once, not a description of an end state. Confusing the two is exactly the distinction Lesson 1 draws between an imperative CLI script and a declarative Terraform or Bicep file.

questions.code:
$ terraform apply
...
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

$ terraform apply
# (no code changes made in between)
questions.prompt: The same configuration is applied a second time with no code changes in between. What happens, and why?
options: Nothing happens — Terraform compares the desired state to what already exists and finds they already match, so there's nothing to do
The two resources are destroyed and recreated identically
Terraform errors out, since the resources already exist from the first apply
Terraform re-runs every step again, taking the same amount of time as the first apply
questions.explain: This is idempotency in practice: because Terraform is declarative, running the same configuration twice with no changes produces the same result both times — a no-op the second time, since the real infrastructure already matches what the code describes.

questions.prompt: A team is already running workloads on both Azure and AWS and wants to provision infrastructure on both using the same tool and the same language. Which tool fits, and why?
options: Terraform, because its HCL syntax and CLI can provision resources on either platform just by swapping which provider plugin is loaded
Bicep, because it compiles to ARM JSON, which AWS also accepts natively
Bicep, because the Azure CLI it depends on can authenticate against AWS as well
Terraform, because it has no state file to keep in sync across two clouds
questions.explain: Terraform's core pitch is portability: the same HCL syntax and `terraform` CLI work against Azure, AWS, GCP, or dozens of other providers, just by loading a different provider plugin. Bicep was built by Microsoft to target Azure only, on purpose — it has no path to provisioning AWS resources at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Terraform vs. Bicep, per Lesson 2.
options: Terraform can provision resources across Azure, AWS, GCP, and other providers by swapping which provider plugin is loaded
Bicep compiles down to ARM template JSON, with Azure itself acting as the source of truth for what's deployed
Terraform requires no separate state file to track what it has provisioned
Bicep can provision resources in any cloud provider, not just Azure
Terraform manages its own state file, which you're responsible for storing safely, usually in a remote backend
questions.explain: Terraform's provider model makes it genuinely multi-cloud, and it does need its own state file stored safely somewhere, usually remotely. Bicep compiles to ARM JSON and relies on Azure itself as the source of truth, which is exactly why it has no separate state file to manage — but that Azure-only scope is deliberate, not an accident, and it cannot reach outside Azure the way Terraform can.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when real infrastructure no longer matches what the IaC code says it should be, that mismatch is called ________.
questions.explain: Drift is exactly that gap — real infrastructure diverging from what the code describes, whether from a manual Portal change, an out-of-band script, or anything else that bypassed the IaC tool.

questions.prompt: Match each command from Lesson 3's tool-installation check to what it actually confirms.
right: Authenticates the Azure CLI against your Azure account
Confirms which subscription is currently active
Confirms the Terraform CLI is installed and reports its version
Confirms the Bicep CLI component is installed and reports its version, separate from the Azure CLI's own version
questions.explain: terraform version confirms the standalone Terraform binary is on your PATH. az bicep version confirms Bicep, installed as an az component, on its own release cadence. az login authenticates the Azure CLI. az account show confirms which subscription is currently active — important once you have more than one and don't want to provision into the wrong one.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of wiring up the azurerm provider, per Lesson 4, in the correct order.
items: Declare a required_providers block naming azurerm and a version constraint
Add a provider "azurerm" block with an empty features {} block
Run terraform init to download the provider plugin matching the version constraint
Terraform records the exact resolved provider version in .terraform.lock.hcl
questions.explain: The required_providers block declares which provider and version range you need; the provider block configures it (even an empty features {} is required); terraform init then downloads the plugin that satisfies the constraint; and the lock file records the exact version it resolved to, so the same version is used everywhere the configuration is applied.

questions.prompt: Two engineers on the same team each write a resource block for an azurerm_storage_account using the local name "example". Does this conflict, and why or why not?
options: No conflict, as long as each block's actual `name` attribute value differs — a local name only needs to be unique within that engineer's own configuration files
It conflicts immediately, because local names must be globally unique across every Azure subscription
Terraform silently renames one of the blocks during apply to resolve the collision
The second configuration fails to parse, because local names must be unique within the Terraform Registry
questions.explain: The local name (`example`) is how one configuration's files refer to a resource block — it's scoped to those files only, and Azure never sees it. The real Azure resource name is the `name` attribute inside the block, and that's the value that has to be valid and, for storage accounts, globally unique. Two different local names set to "example" in two unrelated configurations don't conflict with each other at all.

questions.prompt: This same configuration needs to provision into both a dev and a staging resource group, differing only in name. Which approach matches what Lesson 7 teaches, without editing the .tf file itself for each environment?
options: Override the variable at apply time, either with -var on the command line or a separate .tfvars file per environment
Hardcode the staging resource group name directly inside the resource block, replacing the default
Copy the entire configuration file and rename the resource group in the copy
Declare two separate resource blocks inside the same file, one per possible environment
questions.explain: A `variable` block is exactly what lets the same configuration file produce different environments just by changing one input — overriding it with `-var` or a per-environment `.tfvars` file, never by hand-editing the file itself. That's what guarantees the dev and staging runs differ only in the values intentionally changed.

questions.prompt: This Fabric Capacity resource block is applied with administration_members left empty, as shown. What's the practical consequence, per Lesson 9?
options: The capacity gets created, but nobody — including the person who ran apply — can manage it afterward
The apply fails immediately with a validation error, since the field is secretly required
Terraform automatically adds the currently logged-in Azure CLI user as the administrator
The capacity defaults to being publicly accessible to the entire Azure tenant
questions.explain: The provider marks administration_members as optional, but Lesson 9 is explicit that a Fabric Capacity with no administrators is a capacity nobody can manage after apply finishes. That's why the example instead uses a data source — `data "azurerm_client_config" "current" {}` — to supply a real identity automatically, rather than leaving the list empty.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about provisioning an Event Hub with Terraform, per Lesson 10.
options: azurerm_eventhub must reference its namespace through namespace_id, not a namespace name string
Terraform infers that the namespace must be created before the Event Hub, because the Event Hub's block reads the namespace resource's id attribute
partition_count can be freely increased or decreased at any time after the Event Hub is created
The namespace's sku (Basic, Standard, or Premium) affects what capacity (throughput units) even means
An Event Hub can be provisioned on its own, with no namespace resource declared at all
questions.explain: The Event Hub links to its namespace by the namespace's actual `id` attribute, which is what creates the dependency edge Terraform uses to order creation — no namespace name string, and no separate depends_on needed. partition_count is set once at creation, not freely adjustable afterward. The namespace's sku changes what capacity (throughput units) even means and whether features like Auto-Inflate exist. An Event Hub always comes in a namespace/hub pair — it can't be provisioned alone.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Terraform modules, per Lesson 11.
options: A module is just a folder of .tf files with its own variable and output declarations
A resource defined inside a module but never exposed as an output is still directly readable from outside that module
Fixing a bug inside a module's main.tf automatically applies to every environment that calls it, the next time apply runs
Each module block in the root configuration can pass different variable values, such as a different environment name
A module's source argument must always point at the Terraform Registry, never a local folder
questions.explain: A module is nothing more exotic than a parameterized folder of .tf files. A resource inside it that isn't declared as an output simply isn't reachable from outside — that's the whole point of the module's interface being only its inputs and outputs. Because of that, fixing a bug inside the module's own file benefits every caller automatically on the next apply. And `source` can just as easily point at a local folder (`./modules/data-landing-zone`), which is exactly what Lesson 11's own example does.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike a resource group's name, an Azure Storage Account's name attribute must be ________ across all of Azure, not just within one subscription.
acceptedAnswers: globally unique across all of azure
questions.explain: Storage account names share one namespace across every Azure customer, not just your own subscription — on top of being lowercase-only and 3 to 24 characters, which is why Lesson 8 builds the name from a variable instead of a fixed literal string.

questions.prompt: Match each Event Hub term to what it actually controls, per Lesson 10.
right: Retention window in days for events in the hub
The number of partitions for parallel consumption, set at creation
The container resource an Event Hub is provisioned inside
The Event Hub resource itself, linked to its namespace by namespace_id
questions.explain: azurerm_eventhub_namespace is the container resource an Event Hub lives inside. azurerm_eventhub is the hub itself, linked by namespace_id. partition_count sets the number of partitions at creation. message_retention sets the retention window in days — exactly the concepts Fabric Lesson 20 introduced, now mapped to Terraform arguments.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of provisioning a resource group and a storage account with Terraform, per Lessons 6 and 8, in the correct order.
items: Write a resource block for azurerm_resource_group with a name and location
Write a resource block for azurerm_storage_account that references the resource group's name and location attributes
Run terraform init to download the azurerm provider
Run terraform plan to preview that both resources will be created
Run terraform apply and type yes to confirm
questions.explain: The resource group block is written first since the storage account's block references its attributes, which is also what tells Terraform the build order. terraform init downloads the provider those blocks need. terraform plan previews the two creates before anything happens, and terraform apply, confirmed with yes, actually creates them — exactly the workflow Lesson 8 runs end to end.

questions.prompt: What does the `param` keyword declare in a Bicep file?
options: A value supplied when the file is deployed — Bicep's equivalent of a Terraform variable block
A computed value derived from another expression inside the file, never supplied from outside
A symbolic name used only to reference a resource within the same file
A decorator that restricts which values a resource type's property accepts
A secret value that is never logged, used exclusively for resource names
The ARM API version a resource type targets
questions.explain: `param` declares a value supplied at deployment time, either with a default a caller can override or with no default at all when a sensible default can't exist (like a globally-unique storage account name) — exactly Bicep's equivalent of Terraform's `variable` block from Lesson 7.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Bicep's `var` keyword, not `param`. `var` computes a value from inside the file and is never supplied externally, while `param` is supplied by whoever runs the deployment — mixing the two up is exactly the distinction Lesson 13 draws between them.

questions.code:
az deployment group create \
  --resource-group data-platform-dev \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters storageAccountName=dataplatformdevsa01 \
  --what-if
questions.prompt: This deployment is run with --what-if before running it for real. What does that flag actually do?
options: It reports exactly what would be created, modified, or left unchanged, without touching any real resource
It creates the resources in a temporary sandbox subscription for testing
It skips parameter validation entirely to make the dry run faster
It automatically rolls back the deployment if any single resource fails
questions.explain: --what-if is Bicep's version of the same dry-run idea Terraform's plan gives you (Lesson 18 covers Terraform's side of this): it reports the real diff of what would change, without touching anything, so you can review it before committing to a real deployment.

questions.prompt: Why is sqlAdminPassword declared with the @secure() decorator rather than as a plain string parameter with a default value?
options: @secure() keeps the value from ever being logged in deployment history or output, whereas a plain string parameter risks exposing or hardcoding a real password
@secure() is required by Azure on every parameter in every Bicep file, regardless of what it holds
@secure() makes the parameter optional, while a plain string parameter would be mandatory
@secure() automatically rotates the password after each deployment completes
questions.explain: @secure() tells Bicep never to log or output that value anywhere, and it must be supplied at deploy time rather than hardcoded with a default — exactly the protection a real administrator password needs, which a plain string parameter with a default would not provide.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Bicep and the ARM templates underneath it, per Lessons 12 and 16.
options: Bicep compiles down to the same ARM template JSON format it was always going to become
A Bicep resource's symbolic name, like storageAccount, is the actual name Azure assigns to the resource
az bicep decompile converts an existing ARM template JSON file into Bicep syntax
When one resource's property references another resource's symbolic name, Bicep infers the dependency automatically, with no separate dependsOn needed
Exporting a resource group's template from the Azure Portal always produces a Bicep file directly, never raw ARM JSON
questions.explain: Bicep is an authoring layer over the exact same ARM JSON deployment engine, and az bicep decompile converts existing ARM JSON into that friendlier syntax. A referenced symbolic name creates an automatic dependency with no explicit dependsOn needed. A resource's symbolic name is only used within the Bicep file itself — the actual Azure resource name is the separate `name:` property. And the Portal's "Export template" feature always produces raw ARM JSON, never Bicep.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in Bicep, a ________ — the `@` syntax, as in @allowed or @minLength — restricts what values a parameter accepts, catching a bad value before deployment instead of after.
questions.explain: A decorator like @allowed([...]) or @minLength(3) constrains a parameter's valid values, and VS Code's Bicep extension flags a violation in the Problems pane immediately, before any deployment command ever runs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Azure SQL Bicep example, the database resource declares itself as a child of the server resource with `________: sqlServer`, the same automatic-dependency mechanism as a property reference between resources.
questions.explain: `parent: sqlServer` tells Bicep the database can't exist before the server does, without an explicit dependsOn — the same automatic-dependency inference Lesson 12 introduced, applied here to a parent/child resource pair instead of a plain property reference.

questions.prompt: Match each command or term from Lesson 16 to what it actually does.
right: Runs a Bicep or ARM template against a specific existing resource group
Converts an existing ARM template JSON file into Bicep syntax
Compiles a .bicep file into the ARM template JSON it deploys as
Always produces raw ARM JSON when exporting a resource group's current state, never Bicep
questions.explain: az bicep build compiles .bicep into ARM JSON. az bicep decompile goes the other direction, turning existing ARM JSON into Bicep. The Portal's Export template feature always produces raw ARM JSON. And az deployment group create is the command that actually runs a Bicep or ARM template against an existing resource group.

questions.prompt: A teammate's laptop holding the only copy of terraform.tfstate is lost, and the project had been using local state. What's the direct consequence?
options: Terraform no longer has any record of what it created, so the next apply may try to create duplicates of resources that already exist in Azure
Azure automatically deletes every resource that laptop's Terraform had provisioned
The azurerm provider rebuilds the state file automatically by scanning resource tags
Nothing changes, since Azure itself tracks every Terraform-managed resource independently of any state file
questions.explain: The state file is Terraform's only memory of what it has already built. Lose it, and the next plan has no baseline to compare against — it may propose creating resources that already exist in Azure, on top of the real ones. This is exactly the local-state risk Lesson 17 uses to motivate a remote backend.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about terraform plan, apply, and import, per Lessons 18 and 19.
options: terraform plan compares the .tf files, the current state file, and what's actually deployed in Azure
terraform apply asks for confirmation before changing anything, and typing anything other than "yes" cancels it
terraform import automatically writes the matching resource block into your .tf file for you
Running terraform plan immediately after an import with no diff shown means your resource block matches what's actually deployed
A "~" in plan output means a resource will be destroyed
questions.explain: plan's three-way comparison (code, state, real infrastructure) is exactly what lets it compute a real diff. apply only proceeds on a literal "yes." terraform import does not write your resource block for you — you write it first, then import binds it to the real ID in state, which is exactly why plan right afterward is the check that confirms the block actually matches reality. "~" means update in place; "-" is the symbol for destroy.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the CI/CD workflow, Azure credentials for the azurerm provider are stored as GitHub Actions ________, injected as environment variables at run time, never committed to a .tf file.
questions.explain: A service principal's client ID, secret, tenant ID, and subscription ID live as GitHub Actions secrets, injected as environment variables only when a workflow actually runs — reusing the same credential-handling discipline Git/GitHub/CI-CD Lesson 23 already covered, applied here to infrastructure instead of application code.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a terraform plan output to what it reports, per Lesson 18.
left: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
right: The summary line reporting the total count of each action type
A resource will be updated in place
questions.explain: + marks a resource that will be created, ~ marks one that will be updated in place, and - marks one that will be destroyed. The summary line at the end totals up each of those action types across the whole plan.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of safely importing an existing, hand-created resource into Terraform, per Lesson 19, in the correct order.
items: Confirm the resource's real Azure ID, for example with az storage account show
Write a resource block in the .tf file describing what you believe already exists
Run terraform import to bind that resource block to the real resource's ID in state
Run terraform plan immediately afterward to confirm the block matches reality
questions.explain: You first confirm the real resource's ID, then write a resource block describing what you believe it looks like, then run terraform import to bind that block to the real ID in state. Import doesn't verify the block matches reality field for field, which is exactly why running plan right afterward is not optional — any diff it shows means your block is wrong about some setting.

questions.prompt: The capstone provisions the Storage Account and Event Hub through a reusable landing-zone module, but declares the resource group and Fabric Capacity directly in the root configuration. What's the reasoning, per Lesson 21?
options: The Storage Account and Event Hub are the two resources every environment needs identically, so wrapping them in a module avoids repeating the same pair of blocks per environment
A module can only ever contain exactly two resources, so the other two resources had to stay in the root
The resource group and Fabric Capacity can't be referenced from inside a module at all
Using a module for all four resources together would have created a circular dependency
questions.explain: Lesson 21 reuses the module pattern specifically for the pair of resources (Storage Account, Event Hub) that every environment needs identically, the same reasoning Lesson 11 introduced. The resource group and Fabric Capacity are declared directly in the root since they aren't part of that reusable, identical pair in this capstone's design.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone, per Lessons 21 and 22.
options: The capstone configuration uses a remote azurerm backend for state from the very start, not local state
terraform plan is reviewed before terraform apply actually creates anything, the same discipline taught in Lesson 18
The capstone introduces a brand-new resource type never covered earlier in the course
Finishing this course completes the entire Advanced stage of the Azure/Fabric Data Engineer path, with no courses left in that stage
The capstone's root configuration calls the landing-zone child module once, passing in a name prefix and location
questions.explain: The capstone configures the remote azurerm backend before the first apply, not as an afterthought, and follows the same plan-then-apply review Lesson 18 taught. Every resource type it provisions — resource group, Storage Account, Event Hub, Fabric Capacity — was already covered individually in Lessons 6 through 10. And per Lesson 22, finishing this course does not complete the whole Advanced stage, since Kafka is still ahead in that same stage.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 22, finishing this course closes out the "provision it as code" skill completely, but does not complete the whole Advanced stage of the Azure/Fabric Data Engineer path, since ________ is still ahead in that same stage.
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that this course sits alongside Git/GitHub/CI-CD and Airflow in the Advanced stage, both already complete, but Kafka — for event streaming beyond a single vendor's Eventstream — is still ahead in that same stage.
